concepts.title: Data Bias and Shift
concepts.one_liner: Machine learning theory often assumes future data is identically distributed as past data, but in reality, discrepancies between training and deployment distributions frequently lead to system failures.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to acquire rules from past data that work well on future data. In the theory of machine learning, it is almost always assumed that the future is identically distributed as the past. In reality, it is almost always the case that this is not true. Many of the failures of machine learning in industry and in society are due to this discrepancy between theory and practice. When a learned system is deployed on data that is unlike what it was trained on, various issues can arise regarding the reliability and accuracy of the model.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard machine learning theory relies on the assumption that training and test data come from the same distribution. However, real-world applications often break this assumption. Understanding data bias and shift is critical for diagnosing why models that perform perfectly in the lab fail when deployed in the real world.
concepts.recap_md: - Machine learning typically assumes training and test data are identically distributed.

concepts.title: Distribution Shift
concepts.one_liner: Distribution shift occurs when training data and test data are sampled from different parts of the total data space.
concepts.content:
Distribution shift occurs when the training data is sampled from one part of the total data space and the test data is sampled from another part. There is a gap between the training distribution and test distribution, which can be visualized as a domain gap.

(see figure: Domain gap between training data and test data in the ColorizeBot example.)

In these cases, we are confounded by a shifting data distribution. Shifting data is the rule, not the exception, and it challenges the probabilistic guarantees we expect over future results.
concepts.motivation_md: In practice, the environment in which a model operates changes over time or differs from the controlled environment where data was collected. Recognizing distribution shift is the first step in building robust systems that can generalize beyond their specific training sets.
concepts.recap_md: - Distribution shift is the discrepancy between training and test data distributions.

slots.motivation: In practice, the environment in which a model operates changes over time or differs from the controlled environment where data was collected. Recognizing distribution shift is the first step in building robust systems that can generalize beyond their specific training sets.

concepts.title: Name That Dataset! Game
concepts.one_liner: The 'Name That Dataset!' game demonstrates that computer vision datasets have distinct styles, making them biased samples of the visual world.
concepts.content:
In the paper by Torralba et al. (2011), the authors propose a game called *Name That Dataset!*. The game consists of matching random images from famous computer vision datasets with their corresponding dataset names. The point of the game is to show that it is easy to recognize the *style* of images and to identify the dataset they belong to. If the datasets were unbiased samples of the same visual world, it would be impossible to win the game; however, researchers can correctly match them about 75 percent of the time.

(see figure: Let's play the *Name That Dataset!* game. Modified from @Torralba2011. The game consists in associating each set of three images with the name of the dataset, from the list on the right, they belong...)
concepts.motivation_md: This game serves as a pedagogical tool to prove that datasets are not neutral representations of reality. By showing that humans can identify a dataset just by looking at a few images, it highlights the inherent 'signature' or bias present in data collection processes.
concepts.recap_md: - Researchers can identify specific datasets with high accuracy based on image style.

concepts.title: The Value of Training Examples
concepts.one_liner: The market value of a training example varies across datasets, often requiring more data to achieve the same performance when testing on a different distribution.
concepts.content:
The value of a training example from one dataset can be measured by its effectiveness when used to test on another. A value of 0.25, for instance, means that you need 4 times more training examples than when using a sample derived from the same testing distribution. This 'Market Value' for specific categories, such as a 'car' sample, shows how datasets like LabelMe, PASCAL, ImageNet, and Caltech101 relate to one another in terms of cross-dataset generalization.

|                     | LabelMe market | PASCAL mkt. | ImageNet mkt. | Caltech101 mkt. |
|---------------------|----------------|-------------|---------------|-----------------|
| 1 LabelMe is worth  | 1 LabelMe      | 0.26 Pascal | 0.31 ImageNet | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 Pascal is worth   | 0.50 LabelMe   | 1 Pascal    | 0.88 ImageNet | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 ImageNet is worth | 0.24 LabelMe   | 0.40 Pascal | 1 ImageNet    | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 Caltech101 is worth | 0.23 LabelMe | 0 Pascal    | 0.28 ImageNet | 1 Caltech       |
: "Market Value" for a "car" sample across datasets. Modified from @Torralba2011. {#tbl-market_bias}
concepts.motivation_md: Quantifying the 'value' of data helps researchers understand how much 'transferable' information exists between datasets. It illustrates that not all data is created equal; data from a different distribution is often significantly less efficient for training than data from the target distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Market value measures how many examples from one dataset equal one example from the target distribution.

concepts.title: Photographer Bias
concepts.one_liner: Photographer bias refers to the tendency of humans to capture objects and scenes from preferred, canonical viewpoints rather than random ones.
concepts.content:
Photographer bias is one of the most common biases in image databases and is difficult to eliminate. Studies show that participants have consistent preferences for particular viewpoints of objects, which often correlate with how easy the object is to recognize. People recognize objects better when presented in a canonical orientation.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)

The views recognized faster match the viewpoints preferred when taking a picture. This preference introduces biases in object pose statistics in photographs compared to how objects are actually seen in the world. This bias extends to scenes, involving camera orientation (e.g., the horizon's position), object locations (like the rule of thirds), arrangements, shadows, occlusions, and lighting conditions. Photographers consciously or unconsciously consider these factors when deciding which pictures to take.
concepts.motivation_md: Because humans take the photos used in datasets, those datasets reflect human psychology and aesthetic preferences rather than a raw, objective view of the world. This can lead to models that fail when they encounter objects from 'unnatural' or non-canonical angles.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans prefer 'canonical' viewpoints that make objects easier to recognize.

slots.motivation: Because humans take the photos used in datasets, those datasets reflect human psychology and aesthetic preferences rather than a raw, objective view of the world. This can lead to models that fail when they encounter objects from 'unnatural' or non-canonical angles.
slots.key_passage: - Humans prefer 'canonical' viewpoints that make objects easier to recognize.

concepts.title: Canonical Orientation
concepts.one_liner: A canonical orientation is a preferred viewpoint from which an object is most easily recognized by humans.
concepts.content:
A canonical orientation refers to the viewpoint from which people recognize objects most effectively. Studies have shown that speed and accuracy in object classification are higher when objects are presented in these preferred orientations.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of canonical orientation explains why certain viewpoints dominate image datasets. Understanding this helps identify why a model might be 'brittle' when seeing an object from an unusual angle that was never captured by a human photographer.
concepts.recap_md: - Canonical orientations are viewpoints that maximize recognition speed and accuracy.

concepts.title: Collection Bias
concepts.one_liner: Collection bias arises from the specific protocols or sources used to gather data, such as internet searches or specific capture techniques.
concepts.content:
Collection bias stems from the fact that different data sources—such as egocentric videos, internet images, or vacation photographs—carry significant and identifiable biases. For example, a Google image search for "mug" typically returns images against flat, white backgrounds from canonical viewpoints, rather than the diverse settings where mugs are actually found (like inside a dishwasher or a sink).

(see figure: Pictures of mugs returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)

Such collections often lack diversity, featuring specific traits like handles appearing on the right side or a lack of occlusions. These biases are a direct result of the collection protocol used, such as the ranking algorithms of search engines or the types of images people choose to upload to the internet.
concepts.motivation_md: Models are only as good as the data they see. If the collection process (like web scraping) only captures 'clean' or 'ideal' versions of an object, the resulting AI will likely fail in messy, real-world environments where those objects are occluded or poorly lit.
concepts.recap_md: - Collection bias is the result of the specific protocol or source used to gather images.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: Annotation bias occurs when the choices made by human annotators regarding which images to label and what terms to use introduce systematic errors.
concepts.content: Annotation bias occurs when image annotators choose which images to annotate and which labels to apply. This often correlates with viewpoint preferences and photographer biases, as easier-to-recognize images are more likely to be segmented and labeled, potentially compounding existing biases. Furthermore, the language choices made during annotation are a significant source of bias, particularly social bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Even if the images themselves were perfect, the human act of labeling them introduces subjectivity. Annotators might ignore difficult cases or use inconsistent terminology, which teaches the model to replicate those same human shortcuts and prejudices.
concepts.recap_md: - Annotators tend to label images that are easier to recognize, reinforcing photographer bias.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in data due to collection protocols or existing societal stereotypes.
concepts.content: Social bias can affect both images and their associated labels. It refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. These biases can originate from the data collection protocol or from existing social biases. For instance, images can be captured in certain world regions or contain stereotypes, while labels can reflect social assumptions. An example of social bias is a dataset of images and labels that associates doctors with males and nurses with females. Besides impacting overall model performance, these types of biases can have a negative social impact once deployed. It is important to be aware of these biases and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Social bias exists because datasets often mirror the prejudices and structural inequalities of the real world. If left unaddressed, models trained on this data will perpetuate harmful stereotypes and perform poorly for marginalized groups.
concepts.recap_md:
- Social bias stems from data collection protocols or existing societal stereotypes.
 - It manifests in both image content (e.g., regional representation) and label associations.
 - Mitigation is necessary to prevent negative social impacts and performance disparities upon deployment.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: Biases in the test set can lead to misleading conclusions about model performance and the effectiveness of training data.
concepts.content: While bias is often associated with training sets, biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on final system behavior. The test set is the primary tool researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best or which data collection is more effective. However, there might be little correlation between performance measured on a biased test set and the final performance of the system during deployment. In particular, if we compare two training datasets—one biased and another less biased—by evaluating them on a biased test dataset, we could incorrectly conclude that the biased training dataset is superior.
concepts.motivation_md: Testing and benchmark bias occurs because our evaluation metrics are only as good as the data we use to measure them. If the 'ruler' (the test set) is skewed, we cannot accurately judge which models are truly robust or fair.
concepts.recap_md:
- Test set bias can be more damaging than training bias because it misguides model selection.
 - High performance on a biased test set does not guarantee good performance in real-world deployment.
 - Biased benchmarks can erroneously favor biased training data over more representative datasets.

concepts.title: Bias as a Relative Term
concepts.one_liner: Bias is a relative term comparing two datasets, or a dataset against the real world or a desired distribution.
concepts.content: Bias is a relative term between two datasets, or between a dataset and the real world, or a desired distribution. We only have access to the real world via datasets, which are inevitably biased.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies that 'bias' isn't an absolute property of a single dataset in isolation, but a measure of divergence from a reference point, acknowledging that no dataset perfectly captures reality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Bias describes the relationship between a dataset and a reference distribution.
 - All datasets are inevitably biased representations of the real world.

concepts.title: Adversarial Shifts
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial shifts occur when data changes are malicious and controlled by a competing agent trying to fool a system.
concepts.content: Data shifts can be random, but they can also be adversarial. This occurs whenever the test setting is under the control of a competing agent, such as someone trying to hack a system (computer security), another animal trying to eat us (evolution), or a trader trying to outperform us on the stock market (finance). Neural networks are notably easy for an adversary to fool.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike random noise, adversarial shifts are specifically designed to exploit a model's weaknesses, making them a critical security concern for deployed AI systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial shifts are malicious rather than random.
 - They occur in competitive environments like security, finance, or biology.
 - Standard neural networks are highly vulnerable to these targeted manipulations.

concepts.title: Adversarial Attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to inputs to force a neural network into making specific, incorrect predictions.
concepts.content:
Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking innocuous to a human. The noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. The adversary optimizes the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ to cause a particular output while restricting the noise to a small $r$-radius ball around the original image. For example, to cause a classifier $f$ to misclassify a cat as an ostrich, an attacker finds the noise via:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r
\end{aligned}$$
where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss.

(see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.)

This type of attack requires the attacker to have access to the system to optimize $\mathbf{\epsilon}$. Deploying a system to the public provides this access, making it vulnerable. While simple vulnerabilities can be found manually through architecture analysis or aliasing, large-scale adversarial attacks are generated via optimization procedures to ensure the noise has small amplitude and high confidence in causing failure.
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial attacks demonstrate that neural networks do not 'see' the world like humans do; they rely on features that can be manipulated by tiny, calculated perturbations to cause catastrophic failures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attacks use optimized, imperceptible noise to force specific incorrect outputs.
 - The noise is typically constrained within a small $r$-radius ball around the original input.
 - Publicly accessible models are vulnerable because attackers can use them to optimize their perturbations.

 - The noise is typically constrained within a small $r$-radius ball around the original input.
 - Publicly accessible models are vulnerable because attackers can use them to optimize their perturbations.

concepts.title: Adversarial Robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial robustness is the goal of minimizing a system's worst-case error rather than just its mean error.
concepts.content: Adversarial analysis is worst-case analysis. Typically, systems are trained to minimize empirical risk, defined as the mean error over the training data. Because the focus is only on the mean, the worst case might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, resulting in systems that are more adversarially robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard training only ensures a model works well on average. Adversarial robustness is necessary for safety-critical applications where a single failure caused by a worst-case input could be unacceptable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Standard training minimizes mean error (empirical risk), ignoring worst-case scenarios.
 - Adversarial robustness focuses on minimizing the maximum possible error.
 - It provides a safeguard against inputs specifically designed to exploit model weaknesses.

slots.motivation: Standard training only ensures a model works well on average. Adversarial robustness is necessary for safety-critical applications where a single failure caused by a worst-case input could be unacceptable.

concepts.title: Adversarial Training
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial training increases model robustness by augmenting the training process with worst-case transformations or perturbations.
concepts.content:
Adversarial training is a technique used to increase the robustness of models to adversarial attacks. While standard data augmentation applies random transformations to data to minimize expected loss:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p_{\theta}}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]]
\end{aligned}$$
adversarial training instead considers augmenting with worst-case transformations that incur the highest possible loss:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\theta \in \Theta}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]] 
\end{aligned}$$
In the context of adversarial robustness, one form of this is to set $T$ to be an epsilon-ball attack, $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}$:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\mathbf{\epsilon} \, s.t. \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r}[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}),\mathbf{y})]]
\end{aligned}$$
This increases robustness against perturbations at test time. Beyond robustness, adversarial training is used for generative adversarial networks, reinforcement learning exploration, and competitive agents. It is also known as robust optimization.
concepts.motivation_md: By training on the very examples that would normally fool it, a model learns to ignore malicious noise and focus on more stable, meaningful features.
concepts.recap_md:
- It replaces random data augmentation with worst-case perturbations during training.
 - The objective is to minimize the maximum loss within a defined transformation space (e.g., an epsilon-ball).
 - It is a specific application of the broader field of robust optimization.

slots.motivation: By training on the very examples that would normally fool it, a model learns to ignore malicious noise and focus on more stable, meaningful features.

adversarial training instead considers augmenting with worst-case transformations that incur the highest possible loss:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\theta \in \Theta}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]] 
\end{aligned}$$
In the context of adversarial robustness, one form of this is to set $T$ to be an epsilon-ball attack, $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}$:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\mathbf{\epsilon} \, s.t. \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r}[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}),\mathbf{y})]]
\end{aligned}$$
This increases robustness against perturbations at test time. Beyond robustness, adversarial training is used for generative adversarial networks, reinforcement learning exploration, and competitive agents. It is also known as robust optimization.

prereq.rationale: Distribution shift is a core component of the broader study of data bias and shift introduced in this section.
The 'market value' metric is defined by the effectiveness of training examples when the testing distribution shifts to a different dataset.
Understanding bias as a relative term requires the foundational definition of distribution shift, as bias is measured between different data distributions.
Adversarial robustness is the property of a system being resistant to adversarial attacks, making the understanding of such attacks a prerequisite.
Annotation bias is linked to photographer bias because annotators are more likely to label images that are easy to recognize due to their preferred viewpoints.
Social bias can be introduced or compounded by the labeling and language choices made by human annotators.
Social bias can originate from the data collection protocol, which determines how different groups of people are represented.
Adversarial training is a technique used to increase the robustness of models to adversarial attacks.
The goal of this technique is to achieve adversarial robustness by training on worst-case inputs.
This technique addresses the problem of adversarial shifts where inputs are intentionally manipulated to cause failure.

overlay.rationale: Both concepts originate from the same research (Torralba et al., 2011) and address the problem of dataset-specific biases and cross-dataset generalization.
Adversarial shifts are a specific form of distribution shift where the change in data is intentional and malicious rather than random.
Adversarial attacks are a concrete method used to create the malicious data changes described in the broader concept of adversarial shifts.
Canonical orientations are the specific viewpoints that give rise to photographer bias in image databases.
Collection bias demonstrates how specific data sources (like internet searches) create a distribution shift compared to real-world occurrences.
Collection methods like web searches often inadvertently select for images that exhibit photographer bias.
